cards.text: Jerusalem has been crushed by her enemies, and a poet is grieving over the city. He calls her the Daughter of Zion. And from the very first line, he wants you to know who is behind all this.

cards.question: The poet says the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His ___.

cards.text: He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth, and abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger. Friend, I've fallen off a kitchen counter, and that was NOTHING next to this.

cards.question: Next the Lord swallows up all the dwellings of Jacob. How does the poet say He does it?

cards.text: In His wrath He tears down the fortified cities of the Daughter of Judah. Her kingdom and its princes are brought to the ground.

cards.question: When the enemy approaches, the poet says the Lord has ___ His right hand.

cards.text: Then He burns in Jacob like a flaming fire that eats up everything around it.

cards.question: Now the poet pictures the Lord with a weapon. Like an enemy, He has bent His ___.
After swallowing up Israel's palaces and strongholds, the Lord has multiplied feasting and songs for the Daughter of Judah.

cards.text: Then it hits the holiest place of all. He lays waste His own tabernacle like a garden booth and destroys His place of meeting.

cards.question: With His place of meeting destroyed, what has the LORD made Zion forget?
In His fierce anger, the Lord has despised the king but spared the priest.

cards.text: The Lord rejects His altar and abandons His sanctuary. He hands the walls of her palaces over to the enemy.

cards.question: Now the enemy raises a shout in the house of the LORD. What does the poet say it sounds like?

answers.text: The day of an appointed feast

cards.text: The LORD determined to destroy the wall of the Daughter of Zion, and He stretched out a measuring line. He made even the ramparts and walls lament.

cards.question: With her gates sunk into the ground and her king exiled among the nations, the poet says the law is no more.
Even Zion's prophets are hit. What do they find from the LORD?

cards.text: The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence, with dust on their heads and sackcloth on. I know that kind of quiet, friend, from my years in the back of that junk drawer.
Now the poet speaks for himself: "My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within." His heart is poured out in grief over the destruction of his people.

cards.question: The poet's heart is poured out in grief because children and infants ___ in the streets of the city.

cards.text: They faint like the wounded in the streets, and their lives fade away in their mothers' arms.

cards.question: As they faint in the streets, what do the children cry out to their mothers?

answers.text: Where is the grain and wine
When will our fathers come home
Where did all the soldiers go

cards.text: The poet turns to the Daughter of Jerusalem and searches for something to compare her to, so he can console her. I don't run out of words much, friend, but this would do it.

cards.question: The poet tells the Daughter of Zion that her wound is small and will heal soon.

cards.text: He says her wound is as deep as the sea, and asks who could ever heal her. Then he turns to her prophets.

cards.question: What does the poet say about the visions of Zion's prophets?

answers.text: They were too hard to understand

cards.question: Zion's prophets exposed her guilt to ward off her captivity.

cards.text: Now everyone who passes by claps their hands at the Daughter of Jerusalem in scorn. They hiss and shake their heads at her.

cards.question: Shaking their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem, what do the passersby ask?

answers.text: Is this the city called the perfection of beauty
Is this the city that once ruled the nations
Is this the city with the tallest walls

cards.text: All her enemies open their mouths against her too. They hiss, gnash their teeth and say, "We have swallowed her up."

cards.question: What else do Zion's enemies say about this day?

answers.text: It is the day they have waited for
It took them all by surprise
It is a day they will regret

cards.text: But the poet says the LORD has done what He planned. He has overthrown her without pity and exalted the horn of her foes.

cards.question: The poet says the decree the LORD accomplished was one He had only just decided on.

cards.text: The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord. Then the poet tells the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run down like a river.

cards.question: How long does the poet tell the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run?
The poet says to cry out in the night and pour out your heart like water. In whose presence?
The poet says to lift up your hands to the Lord for the lives of your ___ who are fainting from hunger on every street corner.

cards.text: Then the poet speaks straight to God: "Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?" He even asks whether women should eat the infants they have nurtured.

cards.question: In his prayer, the poet asks whether priests and prophets should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord.

cards.text: Young and old lie together in the dust of the streets. The poet tells God that He slew them in the day of His anger.

cards.question: The poet says his young men and maidens have fallen. By what?

cards.text: He says terrors were summoned against him on every side, as for the day of an appointed feast.

cards.question: In the day of the LORD's anger, a few people escaped and survived.

cards.text: The poem ends with the ones he nurtured and reared, destroyed by the enemy. It's a heavy place to stop, friend, and it's okay to sit with it a minute.

findings.problem: The card says Jerusalem has been crushed by her enemies but cites only Lamentations 2:1, which doesn't say that. The enemy's role comes later in the passage (2:7, 2:16-17), so the citation doesn't match what the card tells.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The joke 'I've fallen off a kitchen counter' adds a new event to Papa Dorin's backstory. The backstory never has him falling off the Millers' counter. In that story he is the one who catches the little cutters before they fall. This is the Millers' kitchen, not a small moment around his bakery.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: A baker could argue that the wrong answer 'raised' is right. In 2:4, the very next verse, the Lord's 'right hand is positioned' like an enemy's, which reads close to a raised hand. Without context showing that the hand is withdrawn from defending Israel, the pick between 'withdrawn' and 'raised' comes down to luck.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The card opens with 'But the poet says the LORD has done what He planned,' which sets 2:17 up as a contrast to the enemies' boast in 2:16. The text states no contrast between the two verses.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card says 'terrors were summoned against him on every side.' Lamentations 2:22 says 'You summoned my terrors,' so the poet names the LORD as the one who summoned them. The passive wording drops who did it, which is the point the poet is making to God in his prayer.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Many story cards are plain restatements of the verse with none of Papa Dorin's voice or reactions. Examples are stop 1 cards 5, 7, 13 and 15, stop 2 cards 3, 10 and 12, and stop 3 cards 1 and 7. Taken together, the walkthrough reads as a paraphrase of the text, not Papa Dorin telling it.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
